I like Jeopardy, and I wanted a data-driven answer to a simple question: of everything the
show could ask me, *what is actually worth studying?* This post walks through how I scraped
40 years of the show, turned every category into something a computer can compare, grouped
the categories into "types," named them, and used the result to find where studying pays off.

Here's the kind of thing it turns up. In **Books & Authors**, the word *Hannibal* appears in
10 of the 60 archived clues whose answer is Mark Twain — because Hannibal, Missouri was his
boyhood home. That's a concrete, learnable association, and the [study tool](research/) this
post ends with is full of them: for any answer that recurs, the specific words the show keeps
attaching to it. Getting there was mostly a data-cleaning slog, and the honest finding is that
the archive is better at showing you *where* the study material is than at ranking topics by
payoff. The rest of this post is how I got there.

Every figure below is generated from a committed dataset — no live scraping — so the whole
post re-renders from scratch.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import plotly.express as px

clues = pd.read_parquet("clues.parquet")
clusters = pd.read_parquet("category_clusters.parquet")
summary = pd.read_parquet("cluster_summary.parquet")
labels = pd.read_csv("cluster_labels.csv").set_index("cluster_id")["name"].to_dict()
tokens = pd.read_parquet("category_tokens.parquet")
tokens = tokens[tokens["era"] == 1980]

plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110
```

## Scraping J-Archive

There's no API, so the data comes from a polite, cached crawl of
[J-Archive](https://j-archive.com): a `fetch` stage (one request/second, every page cached
to disk), a `parse` stage that reads each game's board out of the HTML, and a resumable
`crawl` that walks every season and game. The raw crawl stays on my machine; what ships is
a single compact `clues.parquet` — one row per clue — so anyone (including the CI that
builds this site) starts from identical data without re-scraping.

The result is **563,266 clues** across **9,485 games**, spanning 1984 to 2026.

```{python}
#| label: fig-overview
#| fig-cap: "The corpus: clues per year, game types, and rounds."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4))

per_year = clues["air_date"].dt.year.value_counts().sort_index()
axes[0].bar(per_year.index, per_year.values, color="#4C72B0")
axes[0].set_title("Clues per year")

gt = clues["game_type"].value_counts().head(6)[::-1]
axes[1].barh(gt.index, gt.values, color="#55A868")
axes[1].set_title("Clues by game type (top 6)")

rounds = clues["round"].value_counts()
axes[2].bar(rounds.index, rounds.values, color="#C44E52")
axes[2].set_title("Clues by round")
axes[2].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=20)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## From categories to documents

To compare categories, each one becomes a short text "document": its title followed by its
clue → answer pairs (in a shuffled order, so no clue position carries special weight). For
example, one category instance reads:

```{python}
#| label: sample-doc
#| echo: false
row = clues[clues["category"] == "FISH, BIRD OR MAMMAL"].head(4)
print("FISH, BIRD OR MAMMAL. " + "; ".join(f"{c} -> {a}" for c, a in zip(row["clue"], row["answer"])))
```

Each document is embedded into a 384-dimensional vector with a local sentence-transformer
(`bge-small-en-v1.5`) — a step heavy enough (a GPU-less few minutes over 123k documents)
that it runs offline and commits its *output*, never re-running when the post builds.

## Clustering into "types"

Running K-means (k = 50) over those vectors groups the ~123k category instances into
recognizable *types*. Projected to 2D with UMAP, the map looks like this — hover any point
to see its type, an example category, and that type's most common entity:

```{python}
#| label: fig-clusters
#| fig-cap: "123k category instances, grouped into 50 types (hover to explore; ~4.5k-point sample)."
frac = min(1.0, 4500 / len(clusters))
samp = clusters.groupby("cluster_id", group_keys=False)[clusters.columns.tolist()].apply(
    lambda g: g.sample(frac=frac, random_state=42)
)
samp["type"] = samp["cluster_id"].map(labels)
top1 = tokens[tokens["rank"] == 1].set_index("cluster_id")["phrase"].to_dict()
samp["top_entity"] = samp["cluster_id"].map(top1).fillna("—")

fig = px.scatter(
    samp, x="umap_x", y="umap_y", color="type",
    hover_name="type",
    hover_data={"category": True, "top_entity": True,
                "umap_x": False, "umap_y": False, "type": False, "cluster_id": False},
    render_mode="svg", opacity=0.55,
)
fig.update_traces(marker={"size": 4})
fig.update_layout(showlegend=False, height=620,
                  margin={"l": 0, "r": 0, "t": 10, "b": 0},
                  xaxis_title=None, yaxis_title=None)
fig.show()
```

The 50 types are far from equal in size:

```{python}
#| label: fig-sizes
#| fig-cap: "How common each category type is."
sz = summary.copy()
sz["type"] = sz["cluster_id"].map(labels)
sz = sz.sort_values("size").tail(25)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 9))
plt.barh(sz["type"], sz["size"], color="#4C72B0")
plt.xlabel("category instances")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Naming the 50 types

Each cluster gets an automatic three-part "fingerprint": its most frequent real category
names, the instances closest to its centre, and its most distinctive words (via class-based
TF-IDF). The *fingerprints* are generated; the *names* are the one genuinely interpretive step
— I read each fingerprint and named the type by hand. They came easily enough:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-types
#| echo: false
t = summary.copy()
t["Type"] = t["cluster_id"].map(labels)
top2 = (tokens[tokens["rank"].between(1, 2)]
        .groupby("cluster_id")["phrase"].apply(lambda s: ", ".join(map(str, s))))
t["Example entities"] = t["cluster_id"].map(top2).fillna("—")
t = t.sort_values("size", ascending=False)[["Type", "size", "Example entities"]]
t.columns = ["Type", "Categories", "Example entities"]
t.reset_index(drop=True)
```

## Where the study material is

Two things stand out. First, **wordplay is a big, unusual slice**. The two pure
letter/anagram types — Wordplay & Vocabulary and Rhymes, Anagrams & Common Bonds — are 7.4% of
all categories between them, and folding in Word Origins & Foreign Words brings the
wordplay-and-language family to 10.4%: about one category in ten. It's unusual because it
rewards a *skill* you drill (homophones, anagrams, hidden words) more than facts you memorize,
and it splits into two prep tracks — pure letter games versus the genuinely studyable
etymology and idioms.

Second, the types differ enormously in how much *recurring material* they even offer. As a
rough gauge I count how many distinct phrases recur ≥5 times in a type — drawn from both clues
and answers, taken from raw text before dedup and LLM cleaning, and sensitive to how big the
type is. Crucially, this measures the *breadth* of repeated material, not the payoff of
studying it: a type with thousands of recurring names might take more effort than a small,
predictable one. Read it as "where is there stuff to learn," not "what's the best use of your
time." Entity-dense types (authors, geography, presidents) score high; wordplay and grab-bag
types don't:

```{python}
#| label: fig-applicability
#| fig-cap: "Breadth of recurring material: distinct phrases (from clues and answers) recurring 5+ times, per type."
eras = pd.read_parquet("category_eras.parquet")
eras = eras[eras["era"] == 1980]
ap = eras[["cluster_id", "n_qualifying_phrases"]].copy()
ap["type"] = ap["cluster_id"].map(labels)
ap = ap.sort_values("n_qualifying_phrases")
top = ap.tail(12); bottom = ap.head(8)
show = pd.concat([bottom, top])
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 9))
colors = ["#C44E52"] * len(bottom) + ["#55A868"] * len(top)
plt.barh(show["type"], show["n_qualifying_phrases"], color=colors)
plt.xlabel("distinct recurring entities (count >= 5)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

And for the material-rich types, here are the phrases that recur most — counted across clues
and answers, the stuff worth knowing:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-entities
#| echo: false
def top_entities(name, n=10):
    cid = next((c for c, nm in labels.items() if nm == name), None)
    if cid is None:
        return pd.DataFrame({name: [], "count": []})
    d = tokens[(tokens["cluster_id"] == cid) & (tokens["phrase"].notna())].head(n)
    return pd.DataFrame({name: d["phrase"].values, "count": d["count"].values})

from IPython.display import display
for name in ["U.S. Presidents", "World Geography & Waters", "Books & Authors"]:
    display(top_entities(name))
```

## Cleaning up the entities

Hand-written rules got the entity lists most of the way, but they kept tripping on judgment
calls a regex can't make. Is "John" a studyable entity or a stray first name? ("John Adams"
is; "John" alone isn't.) Is "May" the month or Theresa May? Rules also couldn't tell that
"Sarah of the Clue Crew" is a clue *presenter* rather than an answer, or that a category
about *Grey's Anatomy* had been split into a useless "Grey" and "Anatomy."

So I handed the lists to an LLM for a second look. For each type, it judged every candidate
entity — **keep**, **drop**, or **merge into a canonical form** — with the type's context in
view. It dropped the noise (bare first names, nationalities like "British," months, Clue Crew
presenters) and stitched the fragments back together: "Grey" + "Anatomy" → *Grey's Anatomy*,
"Canadian" → *Canada*, "van Gogh" → *Vincent van Gogh*. Its verdicts live in a committed CSV
the pipeline only *reads*, so the render stays deterministic and I can hand-correct any call
it gets wrong without re-running anything expensive.

A second cleaning pass asked a sharper question — not just "is this a real entity?" but
"does it belong to *this* topic?" That pulled valid-but-off-topic answers out of the wrong
lists: "New York City" is a fine answer, but it's Geography, not **Books & Authors**, so it
no longer clutters the authors list.

A few problems only surfaced on a closer read. A whole rash of bare surnames and first names
turned out to be a *parsing* bug, not messy data: J-Archive writes some answers with an
optional first name in parentheses — `(Henry) Fielding` — and my extractor had been splitting
those into a stray "Henry" and a stray "Fielding." Fixing the extractor at the source
recovered the actual people. The LLM also occasionally over-merged in the other direction:
"Marshall" swept George C. Marshall and Thurgood Marshall into one entry. So a final audit
renamed each over-merged cluster to its dominant person and dropped the remnants too rare to
make a list — while a dedup pass fixed the opposite mistake, fusing one person who'd been
split in two ("Harriet Beecher" and "Beecher Stowe" becoming a single *Harriet Beecher
Stowe*).

## A study tool

The payoff is a lookup tool: pick a category type, see its most common (cleaned) entities,
and jump straight to Wikipedia for each. It's live at [`research/`](research/), and it's
filterable by a cumulative *study window* — all-time, or restricted to clues aired since 1990,
2000, 2010, or 2020 — so you can watch a type's recurring entities shift as you narrow to more
recent years.

Two more touches make it a study aid rather than a lookup: press **Sample clue** to draw a
real clue from that category — highlight an answer first to be quizzed on that specific
entity, or leave it un-highlighted for anything on the board — with the answer hidden until
you ask for it.

Each answer now also carries a **clue fingerprint** — the handful of terms Jeopardy keeps
reusing to ask about it, each with an *N-of-M* count of how many of that answer's clues the
term shows up in, plus real example clues linked back to J-Archive. Tap a cue and, where I
could precompute one, a one-sentence note explains *why* that word points at the answer — why
"Hannibal" belongs to Mark Twain, or "Genoese" to Christopher Columbus. The display even
prefers cues it can explain over generic ones like "author" or "novel," so the fingerprint
teaches the *angle*, not just the name.

For actual drilling there's a **Practice** mode: pick your topics and it deals you a run of
real clues one at a time, answer hidden, with *Knew it / Unsure / Missed* buttons and a score
at the end. This is the one place I built something clever and then tore it out. The first
version was full spaced repetition — Leitner boxes, missed cards resurfacing later in the
session and leading the next one, progress saved in your browser. In use, the resurfacing was
more distracting than helpful: I wanted fresh clues each session, not the ones I'd just
fumbled. So I scrapped the machinery for a plainer deck — *N* distinct random clues from the
topics you picked, no card twice within a session, and nothing remembered between sessions (so
a later session can deal the same clue again). Because the cards are text-only, it also skips
clues that lean on an image or audio you can't see ("the people seen here…").

And a 51st list, **Misc: Hard to Classify**, gathers the categories the
clustering was *least* sure about — the ones that sat farthest from any clean type — so the
oddballs the other 50 lists smoothed over get a place to show themselves.

## So what should I study?

Back to the question I opened with. The honest answer is that the data reframes it more than it
settles it: it can't tell you which topic gives the best *return* on study time — breadth of
recurring material isn't the same as payoff — but it's very good at showing you where the
learnable material lives and handing you the exact angles to learn. If I were actually
cramming, I'd pick one dense, entity-rich type — Books & Authors, say, or U.S. Presidents —
read its clue fingerprints to learn not just the names but the words the show keeps attaching
to them, and drill them in Practice until they stick. And I'd keep the *Misc* pile open as a
humility check: a standing reminder of how much of the board still refuses to be tidy.

```{python}

plt.scatter(s["umap_x"], s["umap_y"], c=s["cluster_id"], cmap="tab20", s=3, alpha=0.5)
```
